scenes.tts: The tallest measured coast redwoods stand more than one hundred metres high. Every leaf at the top gets water from roots in the soil. A tree has no heart and no pump. So what lifts the water? The answer is the dry air around the leaves.

scenes.tts: Water potential predicts which way water moves. Pure water at atmospheric pressure is defined as zero. Water always moves toward lower total water potential. Take illustrative values. Soil is minus zero point three. Root is minus zero point six. Leaf is minus one point five. Air at fifty percent relative humidity is about minus ninety four. Every step runs downhill. The biggest drop is from leaf to air.

scenes.tts: Inside a leaf, water evaporates from the wet walls of the inner photosynthetic cells. The water left in the walls is held more tightly, and its pressure falls. Water moves in from the xylem. Xylem cells that conduct are dead and hollow, a continuous pathway from root to leaf. Cohesion, the attraction between water molecules, lets a thin column in a narrow tube be pulled like a rope.

scenes.tts: Gravity sets a floor on the pull. Water potential rises by about zero point zero one megapascals for each metre of height. A leaf thirty metres up needs zero point three zero megapascals of extra tension just to hold a still column, before any flow. At the top of a one hundred and ten metre redwood, gravity alone adds over one megapascal.

scenes.tts: Could the roots push water up instead? In woody plants and vines, root pressure is small. The highest value in a survey of one hundred and nine tropical vines and woody species was about zero point one five megapascals. That is enough in principle to raise water about fifteen metres. It is weak or absent when transpiration is fastest. Cut the xylem of a transpiring tree, and air is drawn in. Sap does not spurt out.

scenes.tts: A vertebrate heart pushes blood round a closed loop at positive pressure. A typical peak arterial pressure in a resting adult human is about zero point zero one six megapascals. In a transpiring plant, xylem water moves mainly one way, root to leaf, under negative pressure. Evaporation powers it. Xylem water is pulled, not pushed.
